tool_args.old_string: To test whether item dominance is scale-robust, we conduct a within-family analysis using Qwen2.5 at two parameter scales (3B-Instruct and 7B-Instruct) on MMLU under the same BF16 $\times$ 2-temperature $\times$ 6-prompt $\times$ 6-seed $\times$ 4-ordering design. Using a single model family isolates scale as the sole variable. At both 3B (accuracy 0.682) and 7B (0.742), \texttt{item\_id} is the dominant variance component: 75.3\% and 73.4\%, respectively (cf.\ Llama-3.1-8B single-model: 58.4--68.5\% depending on facet crossing). Item dominance is preserved across scales, with minor scale-dependent prompt sensitivity (prompt$\times$item: 12.2\% at 7B vs.\ 8.8\% at 3B). Generalizability coefficients ($G = 0.963$ and $0.956$) confirm that 200 items yield reliable measurements at both scales. Future work will extend this validation to 70B+ models via a fully crossed multi-scale G-study.

tool_args.old_string: Existing studies have examined individual variance sources in isolation, each implicitly assuming separability. \citet{sclar2024formatting} documented up to 76\% accuracy swings from prompt formatting perturbations but held hardware and item selection fixed. BrittleBench \citep{brittlebench2026} found 50\% variance from prompt perturbation under the same constraint. \citet{yuan2025layercast} showed that numerical precision and GPU type cause up to 9\% accuracy variation but provided no factorial attribution to specific sources or their interactions. \citet{messing2026hidden} applied Generalizability theory (G-theory) to LLM evaluation and decomposed variance across five methodology facets on a single benchmark; judge identity dominated at 43.8\%, but the study included no cross-benchmark comparison and excluded infrastructure facets such as numerical precision. \citet{madaan2024quantifying} proposed per-factor variance metrics but did not cross factors. Studies of answer ordering \citep{pezeshkpour2024ordering} and hyperparameter sensitivity \citep{dodge2020finetuning, henderson2018deep} document additional sources in isolation. IRT approaches \citep{polo2024tinybenchmarks, lalor2019irt, zhou2026irt} model item difficulty to construct efficient benchmarks but do not account for prompt, seed, or ordering facets. \citet{bouthillier2021accounting} established ANOVA-based variance decomposition for ML reproducibility, and G-theory has been applied to LLM-based assessment \citep{wei2025gtheory}, but neither crosses infrastructure and methodology facets across multiple benchmarks. Three gaps remain: no study has (a) crossed infrastructure and methodology facets in a unified factorial design, (b) compared variance structures across response formats, or (c) translated variance components into design-dependent reproducibility budgets.
tool_args.new_string: Existing studies examine individual variance sources in isolation. \citet{sclar2024formatting} and BrittleBench \citep{brittlebench2026} documented 50--76\% accuracy swings from prompt formatting; \citet{yuan2025layercast} showed up to 9\% variation from numerical precision; \citet{pezeshkpour2024ordering}, \citet{dodge2020finetuning}, and \citet{henderson2018deep} documented ordering and hyperparameter sensitivity---each holding other factors fixed. \citet{messing2026hidden} applied G-theory to LLM evaluation across five methodology facets on a single benchmark (judge identity: 43.8\%), but excluded infrastructure facets and cross-benchmark comparison. \citet{madaan2024quantifying} proposed per-factor metrics without crossing factors. IRT approaches \citep{polo2024tinybenchmarks, lalor2019irt, zhou2026irt} optimize item selection but ignore prompt, seed, and ordering facets. \citet{bouthillier2021accounting} established ANOVA-based variance decomposition for ML reproducibility. Three gaps remain: no study has (a) crossed infrastructure and methodology facets in a unified factorial design, (b) compared variance structures across response formats, or (c) translated variance components into design-dependent reproducibility budgets.

tool_args.old_string: We address these gaps with a multi-benchmark G-theory study \citep{shavelson1991generalizability, brennan2001generalizability} that crosses up to seven facets (item, model, numerical precision, prompt template, random seed, sampling temperature, and answer ordering) across eight open-weight 7--9B parameter models and five benchmarks (MMLU, ARC-Challenge, HellaSwag, GSM8K, and MATH), totaling 2.3 million records. Our results suggest that the variance structure of LLM evaluation is format-associated. We define \emph{item-related variance} as the sum of item difficulty and model$\times$item interaction (differential item functioning, DIF; \S\ref{sec:gtheory}). Across all three multiple-choice benchmarks, item-related variance concentrates at 68--72\%, while on free-form benchmarks (GSM8K, MATH) it disperses to 31--41\%, with no overlap across the five benchmarks studied. Model$\times$item interaction (up to 36\%) is the second-largest variance source in our multi-facet decomposition, consistent with prior IRT findings on differential item functioning \citep{pezeshkpour2024ordering, polo2024tinybenchmarks}. Models differ not in overall ability but in which specific items they find difficult. This format-associated pattern implies distinct optimization strategies: for MC benchmarks, item pool composition is the primary reliability lever; for free-form benchmarks, model identity and model$\times$prompt interaction matter as much as item selection. D-study projections reveal that multi-facet designs require 10$\times$ fewer items than single-condition designs to achieve $G \geq 0.80$ (55 versus 552 items), with the efficiency gain itself being format-associated across benchmarks. Figure~\ref{fig:cross_benchmark} visualizes the contrast across all five benchmarks.

72	The observed variance structure is format-associated: MC benchmarks concentrate item-related variance at 68--72\%, while FF benchmarks disperse it to 31--41\%, with no overlap. Critically, even restricting to item difficulty alone (excluding model$\times$item DIF), MC benchmarks show 34--38\% versus FF 17--24\%, maintaining complete separation---the format gap does not depend on the bundled metric. A permutation test on \texttt{item\_id} variance shares yields $p = 0.10$ ($n = 5$, $\binom{5}{3} = 10$ exhaustive permutations). The item-level effect size is tightly bounded (Cohen's $d = 1.73$; bootstrap 95\% CI $[1.72, 1.83]$), but the benchmark-level CI spans zero ($[-1.7, 5.1]$, noncentral $t$, $df = 3$), reflecting the inherent limitation of $n = 5$. With $\binom{5}{3} = 10$ possible MC/FF partitions under exhaustive permutation, $p = 0.10$ represents the resolution floor; rejecting at $\alpha = 0.05$ is mathematically impossible regardless of effect magnitude. We therefore present the format-associated pattern as a descriptive observation with strong item-level support ($d = 1.73$ [1.72, 1.83]) rather than a confirmatory finding. This structural difference does not extend to item budgets: GSM8K requires 128 items for $G \geq 0.80$---the highest of all benchmarks---while HellaSwag (MC, 118) exceeds both ARC (MC, 98) and MATH (FF, 101), demonstrating that format alone does not predict evaluation cost. Figure~\ref{fig:cross_benchmark} visualizes the contrast.

tool_args.old_string: To probe the mechanism behind item variance, we exploit the natural heterogeneity within MMLU's 57 subjects. Subjects with higher item difficulty dispersion (measured by $\text{std}(p_i)$ across models) exhibit higher item variance shares, with Spearman $\rho = 0.806$ ($p = 0.005$, $n = 10$ subjects). Notably, \texttt{high\_school\_mathematics}, the only MC subject with open-ended numerical items, shows item variance of just 10.4\%---below the free-form benchmark GSM8K (16.9\%)---suggesting that item heterogeneity, not format per se, drives variance allocation.
tool_args.new_string: One might argue that the format gap is tautological: MC response format constrains generation noise, mechanically reducing residual and inflating item-related shares. Two observations argue against this as a complete explanation. First, HellaSwag is MC yet model$\times$item (36.0\%) exceeds item difficulty (34.3\%)---if format alone determined variance structure, all MC benchmarks would be uniformly item-dominated. Second, within MMLU's 57 subjects, difficulty dispersion ($\text{std}(p_i)$ across models) correlates with item variance share (Spearman $\rho = 0.806$, $p = 0.005$, $n = 10$ subjects), and \texttt{high\_school\_mathematics}---the only MC subject with open-ended numerical items---shows item variance of just 10.4\%, below GSM8K (16.9\%). Format constrains the noise floor, but item difficulty heterogeneity determines the magnitude of item-related variance within that floor.

13	\paragraph{Psychometrics Foundations.}
14	G-theory \cite{shavelson1991generalizability, brennan2001generalizability} provides the canonical framework for multi-facet reliability analysis. Extensions to binary data include \citet{mushquash2006gtheory} and logistic-link generalized G-theory \cite{jiang2018bayesian, tuerlinckx2006glmm}. We operationalize differential item functioning \cite{embretson2000irt} as model$\times$item interaction. Recent psychometric perspectives on LLM evaluation \cite{xiao2025construct, jin2025psychometrics} address complementary concerns of construct validity and measurement properties.

4	On multiple-choice benchmarks, item selection drives 34--38\% of evaluation variance while prompt wording is negligible ($<$3\%). On the free-form reasoning task GSM8K, the structure shifts: model$\times$prompt interaction alone accounts for approximately 9\%, while item selection drops to 17\%. These numbers, drawn from our factorial analysis of 2.3 million evaluation records across five benchmarks, reveal that the variance structure of LLM evaluation is not a fixed property of the pipeline but shifts qualitatively with the response format. Current evaluation practice treats variance sources as independent nuisance factors and controls them one at a time: one study perturbs prompts, another varies precision, a third changes item subsets. This piecemeal approach cannot capture interactions between sources, nor can it predict how the relative importance of each source changes across evaluation settings. Leaderboard rankings built on single-condition evaluations are therefore sensitive to methodological choices that remain unreported and uncontrolled \citep{rodriguez2021leaderboards, dehghani2021benchmark}. No unified factorial framework exists to decompose these sources simultaneously, quantify their interactions, and compare the resulting variance structure across benchmarks.

MATH shows an intermediate pattern with 7 models (DeepSeek excluded): item leads at 24.0\% with model$\times$item at 17.3\%, but residual variance is substantially larger (43.9\%). The exclusion may underestimate model-related variance, as fewer models provide fewer model$\times$item interaction terms; DeepSeek's mathematical reasoning optimization could introduce distinctive interactions absent from the 7-model analysis. The large FF residuals (40--44\%) likely reflect chain-of-thought path diversity, answer extraction variability, and unmodeled higher-order interactions. The dramatic shift from binary $G = 0.936$ to text-exact-match $G = 0.007$ (\S4.1) demonstrates that scoring granularity fundamentally reshapes variance structure. Our format-associated findings are therefore conditional on binary scoring; partial-credit or rubric-based metrics could redistribute FF residual variance and narrow the observed gap.

83	\subsection{Precision Separability}
84	
85	Under binary scoring, BF16 and FP16 are functionally interchangeable: mean accuracy differs by 0.23 percentage points, and all precision$\times$methodology interactions contribute $<$0.1\% of variance \cite{yuan2025layercast}. Under text-exact-match scoring, a precision$\times$temperature interaction emerges at 1.3\%, consistent with the metric-conditional pattern in \S4.1. For standard binary evaluation at BF16/FP16 on single-GPU inference, numerical precision is a negligible variance source that need not be controlled \cite{shanmugavelu2024floating}. For practitioners using non-binary scoring metrics (e.g., BLEU, exact string match), our binary-scoring budgets do not apply. The text-exact-match result ($G = 0.007$, \S4.1) suggests that continuous or string metrics may require fundamentally different---and likely much larger---reproducibility budgets, as temperature-induced variation dominates.

The 7-model MATH analysis may conservatively underestimate model-related variance, as DeepSeek exclusion shifts variance from model×item to residual based on cross-benchmark LOMO trends."

2. **Appendix**: 如有空间，可加一个简表展示 4-benchmark LOMO 结果（加强 robustness 叙事）。如页面紧张则用正文一句话概括。

48	Free-form benchmarks differ markedly. On GSM8K, variance distributes across item (16.9\%), model$\times$item (14.6\%), model (10.7\%), and model$\times$prompt (8.5\%); prompt main effect is 5.4\%. MATH shows an intermediate pattern with 7 models (DeepSeek excluded): item leads at 24.0\% with model$\times$item at 17.3\%, but residual variance is substantially larger (43.9\%). The exclusion may underestimate model-related variance, as fewer models provide fewer model$\times$item interaction terms; DeepSeek's mathematical reasoning optimization could introduce distinctive interactions absent from the 7-model analysis. The large FF residuals (40--44\%) likely reflect chain-of-thought path diversity and answer extraction variability. Since scoring granularity fundamentally reshapes variance structure (binary $G = 0.936$ vs.\ text-exact-match $G = 0.007$; \S4.1), our format-associated findings are conditional on binary scoring.
